stops.name: Toroca, birth in the hacienda lands above Chuquisaca
stops.campa: In the hacienda lands of Toroca, in the hills above Chuquisaca, a daughter is born on 12 July 1780 to the landowner Matías Azurduy, criollo of Basque stock, and his wife Eulalia Bermúdez, a chola of Chuquisaca: Juana. From infancy the girl moves between tongues that are not Spanish, Quechua and Aymara, learned at the fires of the tenant families who work her father's fields. He teaches her to ride and to shoot, skills a hacendado's daughter does not commonly receive, and she takes to both as if the horse and the gun were owed to her.

stops.name: Chuquisaca, orphaned
stops.campa: Juana is seven when her mother's heart fails her suddenly in the family house at Chuquisaca. Her father does not long outlive her: within the same span of years he too is dead, by the account the family keeps, murdered by a nobleman whose name the chronicle withholds, over a matter never made public. The two orphaned sisters, Juana and the younger Rosalía, pass into the keeping of an aunt and uncle, Petrona Azurduy and Francisco Díaz Valle, who raise them by the rule of catechism and obedience rather than the freedom of Toroca's open fields.

stops.name: Convento de Santa Teresa, the enclosure
stops.campa: To settle a dispute over her guardianship and her small inheritance, the family places sixteen-year-old Juana within the walls of the Convento de Santa Teresa in Chuquisaca, the strictest Carmelite house in Upper Peru. She learns embroidery, the psalter, the discipline of silence between offices. But the girl who was taught to ride and to shoot chafes against the grille; she gathers the younger novices to read by candle-stub what the house forbids, the rebellion of Túpac Amaru, the verses of Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, and argues the enclosure's rules openly with the mother superior.

stops.name: Convento de Santa Teresa, the expulsion
stops.campa: After eight months the mother superior has had enough of her. The clandestine readings, the arguments over the rule, the refusal to be made quiet: the convent expels Juana at seventeen and sends her back to Toroca with her dowry unspent and her marriageability, by the city's reckoning, in question. She rides home unbothered by the verdict. What the sisters could not tame in her is the same restlessness that will, within thirty years, be called by the government of Buenos Aires a lieutenant colonelcy, and by the people of two republics a legend.

stops.name: Toroca, the neighbor Manuel Ascencio Padilla
stops.campa: Back at her father's hacienda, Juana falls into the company of Manuel Ascencio Padilla, son of the neighboring hacendado Melchor Padilla and a law student at Chuquisaca's university. Manuel had stood in the crowd that watched the cacique Dámaso Catari executed by the colonial court, and the sight never left him. Between the two young people passes a courtship built on borrowed books: Rousseau, the Encyclopédie, the new grammar of liberty circulating in manuscript among educated colonials who have never seen Paris. They find in each other a rare thing, a marriage of equal appetite for the coming war.

stops.name: Toroca, marriage to Manuel Ascencio Padilla
stops.campa: At twenty-five Juana marries Manuel Ascencio Padilla in the parish of her home country, a match the neighborhood calls sensible and the two of them privately call something larger. Padilla stands beside his wife, on the hacienda and later on the battlefield, in a way the age does not expect of husbands; five children will be born to them in the years that follow, Manuel, Mariano, Juliana, Mercedes, and Luisa, none of them born into a house that will ever again know an ordinary peace. The war that will take four of the five is only four years off.

stops.name: Chuquisaca, the Revolution of 25 May
stops.campa: The Real Audiencia of Charcas rises against its president, Ramón García de León y Pizarro, on 25 May 1809, the first cry of the whole continent's independence, months ahead of Buenos Aires and Caracas. Juana and Manuel, four years married, join the tumult in Chuquisaca's streets; Padilla is marked among the leading conspirators. Within months the counter-revolution, led by General Goyeneche, executes the movement's chiefs and hunts the rest. Padilla flees south into the hills, sheltered village by village by indigenous families who owe him nothing but choose him anyway. The war that will consume them both begins here.

stops.name: Cochabamba, the uprising of 14 September
stops.campa: Word of Buenos Aires's May Revolution reaches Upper Peru, and Cochabamba rises in turn on 14 September 1810. Padilla, hunted since Chuquisaca's fall, enlists under the rebel commander Esteban Arce, given command of two thousand indigenous fighters posted to cut the royal supply road between Lagunillas and Chuquisaca. Juana, hidden with her small children in a succession of safe hamlets, has not yet taken the field herself; she keeps house in secret while her husband's name becomes one the royalist governors circulate on their wanted lists, a debt they mean to collect from his family if not from him.

stops.name: Tarabuco, the arrest and the rescue by night
stops.campa: The net closes after Cochabamba falls. Royalist soldiers seize what remains of the Padilla and Azurduy lands and take Juana and her children as surety against the fugitive husband. Manuel comes by night to the guardhouse near Tarabuco with three horses and cuts the sentries down himself, freeing his wife and sons in the dark before the alarm can carry. From this hour there is no hacienda left to return to, only the hills; the family lives now as its enemies already assume it lives, hidden, moving, armed, a household with no roof but the republiqueta still to be founded.

stops.name: Guaqui, the disaster on the shore of Titicaca
stops.campa: On the reed-fringed shore of Lake Titicaca, at Guaqui, the First Auxiliary Expedition sent from Buenos Aires is broken by the royalist army of Goyeneche on 20 June 1811. The news reaches the hunted families of Chuquisaca province like a second sentence: the army that was to relieve Upper Peru has been erased in an afternoon, and the whole territory falls back under the Crown for a season. For Juana and Manuel, in hiding above Tarabuco, Guaqui means only this, that no help is coming from the south, and that the war they are already living has no near end.

stops.name: La Laguna, the republiqueta begins
stops.campa: In the broken country north of Chuquisaca, among the ranges the country calls Carretas, Sombreros, and Mandinga, Manuel Ascencio Padilla plants the standard of a guerrilla state that answers to no viceroy and, for now, to no Buenos Aires either: the Republiqueta de La Laguna, seated in the town of the same name. From Presto to Tomina to Pomabamba the villages of the department declare for him. Juana is at his side, no longer merely the fugitive's wife but a co-founder of the territory, learning the country's ravines and passes as a general learns a map, because she will soon have to command in them.

stops.name: La Laguna, Juana's apprenticeship of arms
stops.campa: While Manuel rides the republiqueta's circuit, Juana stays at the camp of La Laguna with the children and begins, in secret at first, to make herself a soldier: she sets up straw effigies at the camp's edge and practices with the boleadoras and the lance until her arm no longer tires. Word comes of the women of Cochabamba who threw themselves against Goyeneche's advance with stones and kitchen knives rather than surrender their hill. Between that example and the danger closing on the mountain camp, Juana decides what she has been circling toward since the convent: she will not wait at the fire. She will ride.
